title: The Gilded Age’s George & Bertha Russell Are TV’s Best Couple. Carrie Coon & Morgan Spector Tell Us Why
text:
The Gilded Age’s George & Bertha Russell Are TV’s Best Couple. Carrie Coon & Morgan Spector Tell Us Why

George and Bertha Russell’s marriage is in trouble. In Season 4 of The Gilded Age, the once-unbreakable power couple of New York’s elite are at odds — they’re also an ocean apart. In the season premiere, which aired last night, Bertha (Carrie Coon) is in England with the daughter she married off to a duke after much scheming and plotting as she gives birth to their grandson. While railroad tycoon George (Morgan Spector) is unraveling under the pressure of maintaining an empire and the impending doom of pesky anti-monopoly laws. Last season, he moved out of their house. This season, he’s barely tolerating his wife. It’s a far cry from the doting, sexy, us-against-the-world energy the Russells were giving in Season 1. But the chill between their characters is the exact opposite vibe Coon and Spector exude in real life. 

Together, the actors are warm and playful, complimenting each other frequently and passionately defending their political outspokenness. They sit shoulder to shoulder across from me at the Plaza Hotel in New York City and slip easily from joking about Spector taking up the mantle of Sexiest Man Alive from reigning SMA title holder Noah Wyle to raging about how the arts are under attack and the ills of capitalism. It’s that duality — from silly to serious — that makes The Gilded Age so great. It’s a show about how America has systemically enfranchised its workers and how the uber rich got richer, and it’s a show about the feigned importance of the placement of a salad fork and the etiquette of party invites. It’s about race and class, and it’s about the scandal of premarital sex in the 1900s. It’s about politics and parties. It’s a calming, simple watch with low stakes about frivolous ambition and romance and it’s a commentary on America, racism, gender roles, and the complexity of marriage. 

It’s the latter where Coon and Spector shine. And in our conversation, they make it clear that they are very aware of the chokehold their characters have on the internet. After a slow burn for the series (it barely survived Season 1 but HBO let it cook), the series has now reached peak interest and both actors are the subject of thirst edits and obsessive fan fixation. For those of us who have been riding for the Russells since day one, we welcome the new members to the Railroad Daddy and Opera Mommy hive. I promise those nicknames are earned. Coon and Spector aren’t just ridiculously attractive (obviously), they bring gravitas and glamor to the couple while also lacing the characters with grit, magnetism, and voracity that makes watching them addictive. Here, the pair break down why their characters have struck a chord with audiences, the authenticity of their political statements, and why Coon says Season 4 is “Morgan’s season.” 

I love my parents, George and Bertha Russell! We saw these characters as such a unit for the first season, then last season they were breaking apart, and now they are still at odds. You obviously have a great rapport. Is it fun to play mad at each other or do you miss the unity? 

Carrie Coon: Awww. 

Morgan Spector: Both.  I actually found it so refreshing to be portraying a marriage that really worked, especially in this period.

CC: We were sad in Season 3.  We were fighting a lot in Season 3. 

MS:  Yeah, we were fighting a lot in Season 3. And this season we’re on islands. We’re alienated from each other, and we’re struggling to even communicate at all.  It was delicate charting our routes back to each other this season. That was pretty collaborative so that was fun and interesting and exciting to try to figure out  how do they find their way back to each other?  Why do they do it and what are the moments where they really start to re-solidify as a couple? 

CC:  And in the midst of that, Morgan had this incredible acting challenge of having to figure out charting this addiction story as well.  To me, it’s Morgan’s season in a way that I love. In a way that I’m totally behind. 

MS:  [whispers] You haven’t seen it though. 

CC: I haven’t seen it, no.  But I feel like what was asked of you was the stuff actors dream of. You really rose to the occasion. There was a lot of delight in watching you take that on in a way that we didn’t have in Season 3 of just being in the outs. But this was being able to sit back and admire how you were charting it [and] being proud of you. 

 I love this relationship between the two of you and how much admiration there is. 

CC: It’s real.

It is really beautiful as a fan to see. Last time we talked, you went a little viral for your thoughts on billionaires.

MS: Oh, yeah. 

CC: Oopsies! 

Why has it been important for both of you to speak out about class and be critical of capitalism even though or because you’re playing these characters?

CC:  I don’t know that it’s confined to our publicity for this show. I think Morgan and I have always been politically engaged.  A lot of the actors on this show are. It’s something we respect about each other. We’re theater people. There’s been a war on the arts forever. We are fundamentally hoping for more access to all of the arts and services. Our people are very vulnerable people in the world right now. And so I find that what actually indemnifies you against criticism in some ways is authenticity. The people on this show have kind of always been engaged in that conversation. They’re not suddenly getting involved in it. And I feel like that protects us sometimes from some of the blowback people get when they jump into politics because they have a show that’s suddenly speaking to a moment.

MS: Right. 

CC: And I just feel like we haven’t necessarily been moving through the world that way. Is that true? 

MS:  I think that’s true. A lot of people on our show are politically aware and politically active, outspoken people prior to this show and they will be after the show., I think it is definitely true that for this show, we end up talking about politics during press for this show because the parallels between then and now are so direct and stark.  So it’s impossible not to. Having a group of very politically conscious people who are having to talk about this subject matter, you’re inevitably gonna get commentary  on the present day because it’s just there. 

CC: It’s just the truth.  

When you are watching the show, there are these stark parallels to the present day. George is fighting against monopoly laws this season, which of course has real-word parallels. Is it frustrating or is it hopeful to know these issues have been going on for so long? 

MS: I think it’s really interesting because the rapid urbanization, rapid industrialization, the hyper-concentration of wealth in a small minority. The monopoly capitalism, et cetera, all of that led to massive reforms, right? It led to trust busting. It led to the New Deal in some ways. And it led to huge reorganizations of American society in really fundamental ways. And then we basically forgot all of the lessons of this era. And I think that was basically, you know, there were many factors: globalization, like the sort of offshoring of labor. I mean, we’ve really separated the factory floor and capital, and even the American consumer. Those things all used to be kind of in the same place, and now they’re far-flung all over the globe, often in many different places. And so organizing against the power of concentrated capital doesn’t work the same way it used to. It used to be, you’d have people on the factory floor of a particular factory. In Season 2 — Season Two is our union season, right?

CC: Yeah. [laughs] 

MS: It was — yeah. So, you know, when those guys wanted to shut down your factory, they actually had a tremendous amount of leverage over you. Now, if somebody wants to change, let’s say, Apple’s practices, it’s a factory in Shenzhen or something like that that’s going to have to actually exert that kind of leverage in order to affect an American company. It’s a very different world, but in a lot of ways, I think the results that we’re seeing from the same concentration of wealth, the same concentration of power, are really similar, especially in terms of democracy. Because you cannot have so much power and so much wealth concentrated in so few hands, especially in a political system like ours that is so porous when it comes to money, when it comes to political money, without seeing real destruction of democracy, and I think that’s what we’re seeing. I think our government does not work for ordinary people.

CC: It’s not working for anybody right now.

MS: I think that’s just sort of objectively true, right? There’s a very famous Princeton study showing the preferences of the actual voter versus the preferences of the donors, and the donors get what they want every single time, and the voter gets what they want zero times.

They’re not beholden to us at all. We have really lost control of this apparatus. I think looking to the 19th century, looking to what people did in order to take back some power in similar circumstances is instructive and should be for all of us.

CC:  As a woman, yes, it’s very frustrating. 

MS: [laughs]

CS: Here, here. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 (@refinery29)

 This is why we love both of you. This was also the energy you brought to the billionaire conversation. Carrie, I love how straightforward you are. Let’s take a hard pivot to talk about Railroad Daddy. Now, he’s Railroad Granddaddy. 

MS: Hell yeah. 

CC: Still sexy. 

 How much do you love or hate that nickname and the thirst that happens surrounding the character? 

MS:  What’s to hate? Look, to be sexually objectified as a straight man – a straight white man — is honestly a gift. It’s rare. 

CC:  Move over, [Sexiest Man Alive] Noah Wyle. Next year, Morgan Spector’s coming for you. 

MS:  It’s nice. Train Daddy is another [nickname] and this year, I’m trying to get Trainspotting Daddy started. You know what I mean? Because of the drug addiction going on. Trying to get that started. 

CC: Yeah,  we gotta get that out there. 

MS:  it’s funny. It’s lovely, and I do think it’s the character more than it is me. But it’s nice. What, what can I say? 

Carrie and I are both like, “no, it’s not.” 

CC:  We’re like, “No.” No, no. But keep telling yourself. That’s part of your charm. 

Bertha’s also got stans too! What is it about her that people love so much?

CC: She’s a gay icon! 

MS: [laughs] She’s a gay icon! 

CC:  What’s not to love? Fabulous dresses. So much swagger. It’s the walk.  She’s the ultimate diva. She gets what she wants. She fights for what she wants. She cuts through the BS. She’ll play by the rules until the rules are not serving her, and then she’ll be like, “I see that rule, and I think it’s BS.” And I love that about her. But she also fights really hard for the people she loves, so she has integrity, too. You may not always agree with the way she gets somewhere, but she really is ruthless for her people, and I think that’s a really important quality. And because George and Bertha are fundamentally outsiders and disruptors, we have wealth and power, but we are actually trying to get in, and that is about belonging. Bertha’s fighting to belong, and that’s such an American thing. That’s the spirit of what it meant to come here. We were escaping one sort of tyrannical regime to kind of build a new world, and everyone’s kind of fighting their way in to  have influence and power, and Bertha and George are doing that. And also, her amazing dresses.

MS: She’s fabulous. 

CC:  I mean, she just looks fly. Does anybody say that anymore?  I feel like that was a ’90s holdover and I was like in In Living Color all of a sudden. 

MS: We’re children of the ’90s so we’re allowed. We can keep saying it.

title: Trump Wants You to Believe Non-Citizens Can Vote. They Can’t (But They’re Counting on You To)
text:
Trump Wants You to Believe Non-Citizens Can Vote. They Can’t (But They’re Counting on You To)

Throughout President Donald Trump’s latest term in office, he has alleged that undocumented immigrants vote en masse in U.S. elections, framing the group, which can’t legally vote in federal or state elections, as the key culprits behind a widespread voting fraud scheme in the country. The truth: While this myth persists, the numbers show that election fraud, in general, is very rare. According to a report from The Brennan Center, reported cases of voter fraud amount to less than 1%. And the number of non-citizens who vote illegally is even smaller.

I would know. I became a green card holder in the spring of 2026, which means I still have years to wait before I can take the final steps toward U.S. citizenship and begin voting.  

Since 1996, federal law has made it illegal for non-citizens to vote in federal elections, including presidential and congressional races for the U.S. House and Senate. Knowingly voting in a federal election as a non-citizen can carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and serious immigration consequences, including deportation. Even more, knowingly and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register to vote or cast a ballot in any federal, state, or local election is a federal crime punishable by up to five years in prison.

But that hasn’t stopped Trump, or the Republican party more broadly, from spreading false narratives about immigrants, especially Latine immigrants, and elections. 

“This is part of a wider strategy we’ve been seeing in the past two years, by instilling fear, intimidation, and attacking our democracy,” Carmen M. Feliciano, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy at UnidosUS, tells Refinery29 Somos. 

In asserting these election myths, Trump and his party not only spread misinformation about Latine immigrants, but they also make his supporters suspicious of Latines altogether, questioning the status and legality of Latine citizens waiting to cast their ballot on Election Day.

“The reality is out of 10 Latinos right now in the United States, eight are U.S. citizens. … Every 30 seconds, a Latino citizen turns 18 and becomes eligible to vote,” Feliciano says. “We are a growing population. We are a force to reckon with. … We know that our community can change the election results if we go out to vote and exercise our constitutional right to vote.”

But this requires those in our community with U.S. citizenship to hit the polls. About 50.6% of eligible Latine voters actually voted in the 2024 Presidential Election. And while that percentage is higher than in past races, it still fares lower than other racial or ethnic groups. In fact, eligible non-Latine white voters have a turnout rate of 70.5%, non-Latine Black voters have a turnout rate of 59.6%, and Asian-Americans a turnout rate of 57.1%.

Voting is an act of labor and should be a symbol of commitment to a community we care for. 

Why Non-Citizens Need Citizens to Vote

I can’t vote yet, but if you can, do it — we need you to. 

Since returning to office, the Trump administration has dramatically expanded its efforts to target, harass, detain, and deport immigrants. It has ramped up Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and arrests in communities across the country, expanded fast-track deportations that can bypass immigration court hearings, increased immigration detention, and moved to strip temporary protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants. It has also targeted asylum access and even birthright citizenship. The result is an increasingly hostile and uncertain environment for immigrants, not just those without legal status, but also people with temporary protections, legal residency, and families with mixed immigration statuses.

And it’s not just immigration policies. Like U.S. citizens, non-citizens are navigating an increasingly expensive cost of living, worrying about everything from groceries and rent to healthcare and the cost of raising children.

One issue I’m especially concerned about is the potential substantial changes coming in the 2030 census, like Trump’s plan to remove race and ethnicity questions and data. This is dangerous. Latine nonprofits, grassroots organizations, and even Hispanic-Serving-Institutions (HSIs) in higher education cannot function or sustain without grant-funded programs or community-based financial support. A census undercount for Latines can mean fewer resources for schools, clinics, and local infrastructure, which affects citizens and non-citizens alike. 

Last month, I wrapped up my role as a program assistant at an HSI that serves mostly Latine and Black American students. As of September 30, that institution, Saint Peter’s University, one of the most relevant HSIs in the Latine-dense area of Jersey City, New Jersey, closed down the wellness and educational initiatives of the Bienestar For All program, a $3 million federal Title V grant-funded project from the  U.S. Department of Education – a devastating loss for my team and our students, most of whom are food insecure and lack the adequate wellness education they need to succeed in college. 

“Our younger generation needs to understand that voting is necessary to express our opinions. It is a sacred right at the base of our democracy,” Feliciano says.

So when you hit the polls for the midterms, remember those of us who can’t, those who are disenfranchised even while we’re being disparaged. When you vote, take your family, your friends, and your neighbors. Make a day out of it. Bring snacks, bring music, and make the trip something people look forward to rather than something they dread. There will be lines, and that’s okay. Wait through them. If you’re worried about making it before the polling place closes, don’t let that discourage you. In most states, if you’re already standing in line when the polls close, you still get to cast your ballot. 

And when the day is over, keep going. Follow trusted pages and publications that cover these issues, ideally bilingual ones, so that nobody in your household gets left out of the conversation. Learn how local, state, and federal politics work and get involved beyond voting. 

“Know who your member of Congress is, who is your senator. How do they represent you? Go to a town hall meeting. Ask questions. Every member of Congress has a district office. They’re not in D.C. all the time. Every week members of Congress go back to their district office, and as a constituent, you have the right to go to their offices and ask questions. They owe you a response,” Feliciano adds.

Be responsible with your political conscience, because it’s one of the most powerful things you have. 

How Non-Citizens Can Show Up Even Though We Can’t Vote

While non-citizen Latines can’t vote, there are other ways we can show up. Beyond the ballot, green card or visa holders, just like any other immigrant with any kind of official documentation, can still take part in civic life. They can volunteer, organize, attend public meetings, speak at town halls, protest, and support civic engagement groups, especially those with a grassroots structure. 

Johanna Toruño, artist and founder of the public art project The Unapologetic Street Series, does not let her immigration status stop her from civic engagement. “As a person who can’t vote in this country yet, I’ve found ways to feel involved because it can feel quite daunting to not be able to participate in the decision-making,” the El Salvador-born, Los Angeles-based artist tells Somos. “I canvass, volunteer my time to campaigns I believe in, and organize with neighbors and friends to push voters to do exactly that — engage.” 

Toruño also gets real with her community about the ways misinformation and religious conservatism impacts the ways in which they vote. “Latines tend to be more conservative and vote against their interests, and even their own values at times, because political appearances matter more,” she shares with Somos. 

She points out that religious conservatism, for instance, which is prevalent across Latin America and the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, doesn’t translate the same way in U.S. politics because “the privileges some Latines have in their home countries to allow them to be so conservative don’t apply here in the same way, but still they vote as such.” 

As a Brazilian, I saw this recently amid those living in the U.S. who cast their ballot in our homeland’s most-recent presidential election, with 62.7% of Brazilian immigrants preferring Evangelical right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro over his leftist counterpart, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

“I’d like Latines to explore those themes in their voting practices, especially because so many of us come from mixed-status families who pay the consequences for it, even if they agree,” Toruño adds.

Like Toruño, while I can’t vote in this year’s elections, as a green card holder, I have options to show up and forge my political voice in the best and most formative ways I can. For instance, as an adjunct lecturer in the New York City metropolitan area, I have been adapting my school curriculum and giving extra time to go over the rights and impacts of voting in class with my college students, especially since the majority of them are Latine as well. 

A passive citizen is a person who’s depriving themselves of a future with better and brighter possibilities. But political apathy can show up for those of us who are on a temporary hold, too. Our status can’t be the source of stagnant behavior. I understand it is my responsibility to be informed and to cultivate a sense of belonging with what I can learn from local, state, and national politics, even as an immigrant. Latine immigrants like Toruño are an example of how we can maximize our resources to build a sustainable future with informed and curated knowledge around politics, community care, and social justice values.

I’m showing up how I can. I’m still waiting for my turn to vote, but when it comes, when I become a U.S. citizen, I’ll show up the way I’m asking you to show up now. Because we matter. We always have, and we always will.

Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why November opens with the dead, particularly our ancestors and beloved spirit guides. On November 1 and 2, Día de Muertos fills homes with marigolds, candles, and the favorite foods of those who came before us. At the same time, in Haiti and across its diaspora, Fèt Gede honors the Gede, the spirits of death in Haitian Vodou. They’re known for their dark humor, their unapologetic sexuality, and their power to heal. Neither tradition treats death as something to fear. Both treat it as part of life, a doorway, and a reason to celebrate.

This month, we are also deep in Scorpio season, ruled by the very things most people avoid talking about: death, desire, and transformation. Scorpio knows that nothing is reborn without first being let go, and that pleasure and power live in the places we’ve been taught to hide. The New Moon in Scorpio on November 9 plants the seed of who you’re becoming. Meanwhile, on November 13, Venus and Mercury both station direct, ending the review of your love life and your truth that began in October. What you learned in the dark is now ready to be lived.

Death, sex, and rebirth aren’t taboo. They’re sacred themes that help us embrace more life. Something in your life is ending. Something in you is craving more. And someone new is emerging from what you’re finally ready to release. You can’t fully live until you’re willing to let something die.

title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 1 To 7
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: November 1 To 7

R29 babes, November begins with a much-needed cosmic breather. With no major planetary shifts this week, we have room to recalibrate while Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra continue encouraging us to review our relationships, finances, and emotional patterns. The Scorpio New Moon arrives November 9th, so consider this week your chance to get grounded before the momentum picks up. We start with the Moon in Leo joining forces with Mars and Jupiter, boosting our confidence and reminding us to align our actions with our bigger vision. Less talking about it, more being about it. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo for two and a half days, helping us get down to the nitty-gritty of what needs to be handled.
